questions.stem: An affine variety $V \subset k^n$ is defined as:

options.text: The common zero set of a collection of polynomials in $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$.
options.explanation: An affine variety is $V(f_1,\ldots,f_r) = \{a \in k^n : f_i(a) = 0\ \forall i\}$. Hilbert's Nullstellensatz gives the dictionary between varieties and radical ideals.
Smooth manifolds are objects of differential geometry. Algebraic varieties are defined by polynomial equations and may have singular points where the manifold structure breaks down.

options.text: The image of a polynomial map from $k$ to $k^n$.
options.explanation: Images of polynomial maps (rational curves) are a special type of variety but not the definition of varieties in general.

options.text: A subset of $k^n$ closed in the Euclidean topology.
options.explanation: In the Zariski topology, closed sets are algebraic varieties. But in the Euclidean topology, many more sets are closed. Algebraic geometry uses the Zariski topology.

questions.stem: The genus $g$ of a smooth projective complex algebraic curve corresponds topologically to:

options.text: The number of handles on the corresponding Riemann surface.
options.explanation: A smooth projective curve over $\mathbb{C}$ is a compact Riemann surface of genus $g$: a sphere with $g$ handles attached. $g=0$: sphere; $g=1$: torus (elliptic curve); $g \ge 2$: higher genus surface.

options.text: The degree of the defining polynomial.
options.explanation: Degree and genus are related (for a smooth plane curve of degree $d$, genus $= (d-1)(d-2)/2$) but they are different quantities.

options.text: The dimension of the curve as a real manifold.
options.explanation: All algebraic curves have real dimension 2 (as complex dimension 1 manifolds). Genus is not the real dimension.
Irreducible components is a separate concept. A smooth irreducible curve has genus $g$ for any $g \ge 0$.

questions.stem: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz, over an algebraically closed field, gives a correspondence between:

options.text: Radical ideals in $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and algebraic varieties in $k^n$.
options.explanation: The Nullstellensatz (zero locus theorem) is the fundamental bridge of algebraic geometry. Radical ideals correspond bijectively to varieties; prime ideals correspond to irreducible varieties.
True but weaker: maximal ideals of $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ over an algebraically closed field correspond to points. The full Nullstellensatz covers all radical ideals and varieties.
Prime ideals correspond to irreducible varieties, not smooth ones. Irreducibility and smoothness are different properties.
Algebraic varieties need not be manifolds (they can have singular points). The correspondence is between ideals and varieties (not necessarily smooth).
